title: If Children Were Angels https://www.educationnext.org/if-children-were-angels-the-science-of-discipline-book-review-maynard/
author: Robert Pondiscio
summary: Robert Pondiscio reviews Nathan Maynard's The Science of Discipline, which frames student misbehavior as communication of unmet needs rather than a character deficiency. Pondiscio argues that while Maynard's emphasis on empathy and relationships is valuable, his framework neglects the formative purpose of discipline—shaping identity and character, not just managing behavior. True school discipline builds cultures where good conduct carries status and self-command earns respect.
points: Maynard's 'Science of Discipline' treats behavior as communication of unmet needs, not character deficiency
Pondiscio argues this diagnostic approach neglects the formative purpose of discipline in shaping student character
Schools that reward misbehavior with leadership roles signal to all students that disruption pays off
The deepest discipline system is a school culture students wish to belong to, not a therapeutic enterprise
Both diagnostic and formative approaches are needed; the danger is losing confidence in forming character
quotes: The work of schooling has always involved cultivating the former in students while restraining the latter. Any theory of discipline that forgets or denies this begins in sentimentality and often ends in disorder.
The central question of school discipline cannot be what makes adults feel humane. It must be what best serves children over time.
A discipline system is instructive not only in what it says to the child who misbehaves but in what everyone else learns from watching the adults respond.

The central task of discipline, then, is not endless negotiation over rules nor therapeutic management of every conflict. It is the formation of identity through coherent norms and shared expectations.
The concern is that contemporary discipline discourse has become so focused on explaining behavior that it has lost confidence in forming it.
